Title: Player refusing to give deck list?

Messages.Author: Petri Wessman
Messages.Body:
Ok, I'm in a bit a weird position here. I ran the big Ropecon
tournament for the Nth time last weekend (93 players this year), and
things generally went great. As traditional, I have not demanded deck
lists from players beforehand since I feel that just adds to the
general hassle and provides little benefit, but I've always published
the finalist deck lists along with final round transcript. The
finalists were told (as is normal) before the final round started that
I want them to send me their deck lists as soon as possible (the
finals typically run from about 1am to 3am, so taking time off to
transcribe deck lists at that point isn't a fun option).

To date this has worked fine, but this year there is a glitch. Four of
the finalists send theirs promptly (thanks, guys :), but one I haven't
heard from despite nudges (via Otto). Now I just heard that this
particular guy has in the past refused to give deck lists to
tournament organizers despite being asked by the organizer (apparently
this happened to Otto in the Finnish championships).

Assuming the guy really does refuse to send me his deck list, what are
my options as head judge & organizer? I stated quite clearly that I
want the deck lists before the final round started.

I'm a bit mystified (and somewhat pissed off) here. It looked like a
fairly bog-standard old-school Stanislava & friends deck to me, it's
not like it's the secret to eternal youth or a cure for cancer we're
talking about here. :}

-Petri

We had the same discussion some four years ago (IIRC) when one of the
finalists of the german ECQ didn't want to have his deck list
published. The reason for this was that he didn't want to know other
players the *exact* contents of his deck, at least not before the next
big tournaments. Although if you saw him playing you had a pretty good
idea what the deck actually contained. The head judge & organizer back
then complied to the wishes of the player, although he had the
decklist in his hands and wasn't obliged to follow this player's wish.
The same happened after the First Chance Qualifier during the EC 2009;
here also the organizer & headjudge complied to the player's wish.

I think, as a head judge & organizer you can't make that player give
you decklist here and now. I would suggest that you just move on for
now. In the end the only real chance you have is to make decklists
mandatory for all participants in the tournament (and receive them
*before* the tournament starts). After that it's really hard to
enforce decklists, because it's either impractical (i.e. writing
decklists before the final starts) and/or there are no explicit rules
in tournament rules or the penalty guide for not providing a decklist.

If he's the tournament winner: too bad he's not getting his deck
posted in Lasombra's tournament winning deck archive.

Best regards, Ralf

The head judge or tournament organizer may require players to register

Some gaming groups have a different culture. By this I mean, some
groups have a majority of players who don't want a deck published
until it wins a tournament and sometimes not even then. The playgroup
in Los Angeles has always seemed to operate this way (now I'm going to
get it from those guys!). I remember asking a player at an L.A. tourny

just do it. Its really not a big deal. And if your worried about
losing some prestige when someone else plays a similar deck, stop
worrying, there isn't a "Nobel Prize for deckbuilding in VtES."

On Jul 30, 2:06 am, TorranceCircle <torrance.cir...@gmail.com> wrote:
> The TWDA and any posts or tournament write-ups have always been

Yeah. I'll expand on this: the reason I write a finals transcript and
include the finalist decklists is that it gives a snapshot into what
sorts of decks were played at the winning table of a very large
tournament, and how they were played. A snapshot into the local
metagame of that year, if you will. I think that's very interesting
and educational for other players, both local and foreign.

Also, please remember that "deck tech" isn't a universal constant, it
*heavily* relies on the metagame. A deck that might win the Ropecon
tournament might easily fail totally at the EC. Or vice versa.
Different metagames. It's not like you can "netdeck" something that
has won somewhere and just use it to easily win somewhere else. You
need to figure out how to play it, and also modify it for the local
metagame.

> Some gaming groups have a different culture. By this I mean, some
> groups have a majority of players who don't want a deck published
> until it wins a tournament and sometimes not even then. The playgroup
> in Los Angeles has always seemed to operate this way (now I'm going to
> get it from those guys!). I remember asking a player at an L.A. tourny
> if I could look at and talk to him about his deck because I had a
> similar deck. His prompt reply...."NO!" I guess what I'm saying is; if
> you are at a tournament where the culture is to turn in a decklist
> just do it. Its really not a big deal. And if your worried about
> losing some prestige when someone else plays a similar deck, stop
> worrying, there isn't a "Nobel Prize for deckbuilding in VtES."

Quite. To minimize misunderstandings, tournament organizers should
probably be more clear and specific about their intent to publicize
deck lists (in the tournament announcements etc). Some organizers want
to make the finalist decks public, some want to only make the winner
deck public, some allow for player choice in the matter... making that
stand public beforehand would clear up a lot of things.That way people
who are paranoid about their decks can simply choose not to play in
certain tournaments.

As a side note: while there isn't a "Nobel Prize for deckbuilding in
VtES", there is the kind of fame that comes from having other people
use your deck elsewhere -- polite players attribute the original
creator, and word spreads around. Being the originator of a new "deck
archetype" can be a very cool thing, too.

-Petri

Yeah. Knock me down with a feather, but I agree with you! However, it's
still very silly. Decks do not play themselves, particularly not in a 92
player tournament. As someone who's both copied and been copied, as well
as someone who enjoys borrowing and freely lends decks, I can tell you the
player matters quite a lot.

Now you could memorize (or even write down and carry around) a decklist
and thereby have a significant advantage over that deck should you happen
to see it again, assuming the deck hasn't been changed. But doing this
simply isn't practical. In a 92 player tournament, you're fairly unlikely
to come up against any one player. And assuming it's not a total
noob-fest (and this is Finland we're talking about - vtes is their
national sport), there are no guarantees about which players will be seen
in the final. For my money, doing this is wasting effort on one dangerous
foe at the expense of ignoring the other 90.

Messages.Author: echia...@yahoo.com
Messages.Body:
On Jul 29, 3:46 am, Petri Wessman <or...@iki.fi> wrote:
> Ok, I'm in a bit a weird position here. I ran the big Ropecon
> tournament for the Nth time last weekend (93 players this year), and
> things generally went great. As traditional, I have not demanded deck
> lists from players beforehand since I feel that just adds to the
> general hassle and provides little benefit, but I've always published
> the finalist deck lists along with final round transcript. The
> finalists were told (as is normal) before the final round started that
> I want them to send me their deck lists as soon as possible (the
> finals typically run from about 1am to 3am, so taking time off to
> transcribe deck lists at that point isn't a fun option).

>
> To date this has worked fine, but this year there is a glitch. Four of
> the finalists send theirs promptly (thanks, guys :), but one I haven't
> heard from despite nudges (via Otto). Now I just heard that this
> particular guy has in the past refused to give deck lists to
> tournament organizers despite being asked by the organizer (apparently
> this happened to Otto in the Finnish championships).
>
> Assuming the guy really does refuse to send me his deck list, what are
> my options as head judge & organizer? I stated quite clearly that I
> want the deck lists before the final round started.
>

> I'm a bit mystified (and somewhat pissed off) here. It looked like a
> fairly bog-standard old-school Stanislava & friends deck to me, it's
> not like it's the secret to eternal youth or a cure for cancer we're
> talking about here. :}

#1. It looks like the situation has pretty much sorted itself out.
(But it does touch upon larger issues that I'd like to address)

#2. If the player had refused to send a deck list despite your
official request and despite the official rules, I agree with you that
he is being a bit of a jerk. But some people are okay with being a
jerk and that's fine.

#3. But in my personal opinion, you are also slightly being a jerk
(though not as bad as in #2) by adamantly refusing to consider the
player's perspective. Your main line of logic seems to be that you've
always published all the deck lists in your report ("because I want to

write a tournament report which includes said decks (and final round

transcript), and have done so for ages now"). But you know, it
wouldn't be the end of the world if for once, your report was missing
a single deck list. I'm sure people would get the gist of the tourney
report with a general description instead of an exact deck list.

I do applaud tournament organizers for all their hard work. That being
said, I've known quite a number of tournament organizers (this isn't
specifically addressed to anyone in particular) who are actually also
control freaks. Everything has to be done a special way - their way,
or they get really upset. I can sympathize with that - I can be a bit
like that at times as well. But ultimately, it's a bit self-centered
(which isn't necessarily a bad thing) to expect or force everyone to
do things *your* particular way.

It was mentioned that:

1.6. Publishing Event Information

White Wolf, Inc. reserves the right to publish event information such
as the contents of any player's deck as well as transcripts or video
reproductions of any sanctioned tournament. The tournament organizer
is also permitted to publish event information.

--> Although the rules *allow* tournament organizers to publish deck
information (even without the player's permission), it certainly does
not *require* them to do so. There's a big difference between can and
should.

There are many things that players (and organizers) can do, which are
permitted by the rules, but invoking such a rule is still a jerk thing
to do. Plus, there are plenty of rules which aren't always strictly
followed....

2.4 Spectator Responsibilities

All spectators are expected to remain silent during the course of a
game and are not permitted to communicate with players in any way
while a game is in progress.

--> "Quiet Dave! I'm in a game with Robyn right now and the rules say
you're not allowed to ask for car keys / cell phone / money / hotel
key card / food / whatever. Rules say no communicating at all. Sorry."

Spectators who believe that they have observed rules violations should
inform a judge, but they must not interfere with the game.

--> Oftentimes when spectators observe an obvious rules violation
(sorry, Timothy Crowley can't play superior Govern because he only has
inferior Dominate) they simply point it out. Strictly speaking, the
rules actually prohibit that. They're technically supposed to relay
that to a judge (though most of the time, by the time you've dragged a
judge over and explained the mistake, it's a big hassle to "rewind"
things back to that point).

3.1.2. Preliminary Rounds Seating

The judge will group players randomly and impartially, using prepared
index cards, a computerized system for generating random groupings, or
another impartial randomizing method.

--> Seen several tournaments where judges number players based on
their arrival/registration order (which means that people who arrive
together in the same carpool end up playing at the first table
together).

3.1.5 Multi-Deck System

Players are prohibited from making modifications to their decks
between rounds unless the tournament uses the following multi-deck
rules.

--> Brings up the interesting issue of what happens when Player A's
card (like a Fame) accidentally ends up in Player B's library for the
next round. What sort of penalty should occur? Heck, a really jerky
player could intentionally bring a deck full of cards that get passed
around to other players. Surely some cards will fail to get returned.
Talk about a "Vampiric Disease" deck - you can try to infect everyone
else's libraries with your cards! (Works best if no one plays with
sleeves).

4.1. Cards Allowed

All cards in a player's deck must be genuine Vampire: The Eternal
Struggle or Jyhad cards.

If cards with distinct backs are used in the same deck (e.g., Jyhad
and Vampire: The Eternal Struggle cards, or upside-down 3rd Edition
cards and right-side up cards, or mis-cut cards) are used, in order to
prevent a significant advantage, all cards from the different sets,
printings, etc. must be of sufficiently mixed card type.

--> Strictly speaking, this section does not seem to factor in
sleeves. Based on the wording, a sufficiently mixed combination must
be present even if all the cards are in opaque sleeves.

--> I've never seen the provision used in practice. But a jerky player
or organizer could demand to inspect a deck for sufficiently mixed
card types.

4.4. Card Elevation and Disposition

Players must keep their cards above the level of the playing surface.

--> Never seen anyone invoke this. Say someone has a medical condition
that affects the placement of their hands. Technically, you could
invoke this rule (though you'd be a jerk to do so).

4.6. Card Sleeves

Once a game begins, players may request that the judge inspect an
opponent's card sleeves. The judge may disallow a player's card
sleeves if the judge believes they are marked, worn, or otherwise in a
condition that interferes with shuffling or game play.

--> Never seen this either. But a jerk player technically could make
such a request. (The rules are hazier whether the judge could refuse
to inspect the sleeves. 2.4 specifically allows the judge to refuse
requests involving spectators as they see fit).

4.7. Tapped Cards

If a card must be tapped as a part of the game rules, it must be
turned approximately 90 degrees from the normal position.

--> "Sorry, 45 degrees just doesn't cut it. I want a full 90 degree
rotation." Ha ha. I guess this one doesn't even count as stalling -
it's just invoking the proper rules.

8.1. Sanctioning Deadline

To ensure sanctioning approval, tournament organizers must apply for
V:EKN sanctioning at least twenty-eight days prior to the event.

8.2. Sanctioned Tournament Advertising

Sanctioned tournaments should be announced/advertised at least twenty-
eight days prior to the event. Announcements should include the time
and place of the event.

9.1. Organizer Records

Tournament organizers are required to keep copies of all tournament
reports for V:EKN-sanctioned events they run for a period of one year.
These records serve as backups in case event results are lost.

9.2. Event Report Deadline

Event reports are due to the V:EKN within eight days of the
tournament's conclusion. Tournament reports not received by the V:EKN
within eight days are considered late, and are listed in the V:EKN
tournament database as "Not Received" for fourteen days after the
event.

9.3. Delinquent Tournaments

Event reports must be received by the V:EKN within thirty days of the
tournament's conclusion. Event reports not received within fifteen to
thirty days are listed as "Delinquent" in the V:EKN tournament
database. Organizers may still submit event results in this time frame
without penalty.

--> Even in the old days, these rules were commonly broken.

In the past, some events (like EC's) have had English language rules.
For example:

"OFFICIAL LANGUAGE: Unless each player at a given table speaks the
same language, each player will have to speak English during their
games. In the case that there are players who don't speak English,
they should call a judge as a translator." (This one was approved by
LSJ in 2003 for Spain).

Suppose you're at a table where your prey only speaks Spanish.
Technically, you could demand that he speak English (or else find a
translator). It can be a bit of a jerky thing to do, but the rules do
allow it. Must...speak...English!

--> So yes, the rules do allow you to publish deck information without
consent. But doing so can be a jerk thing to do. Especially if your
only motivation is your OCD / control freak tendency / personal
tradition that *has* to be followed.

I kind of like the idea of tournament organizers organizing the
tournament, and setting the expectations towards players, who can -
based on those expectations - choose whether they want to attend the
tournament or not. Then nobody is being a jerk - the players can
freely choose not to attend, but those attending accept the whole
package.

So simply say in the description of the tournament that decklists are
expected of finalists, so people who don't want to give their
decklists skip out on the tournament altogether.

Then if someone is still trying to be a smartass you can happily
penalize their asses off. It's much better for everyone to punish
that person than to punish everyone in the future (e.g. by
requesting finalists to write up their decklists before the
finals...).

--
Regards,

Daneel

Yes, it seems so. Some nice discussion in this thread (despite some

> #3. But in my personal opinion, you are also slightly being a jerk

> wouldn't be the end of the world if for once, your report was missing
> a single deck list. I'm sure people would get the gist of the tourney
> report with a general description instead of an exact deck list.

Well, my point here is precedent. If I let one person hide his deck
list, I will have to let everyone else do so, too. I cannot play
favorites.

So it boils down to a choice of:

a) require all finalists to give me their deck lists
b) make giving deck lists optional

I simply choose to do (a). Maybe I'm being a jerk by doing so, but
I've outlined "why" in earlier posts. In my opinion, the "general
good" (i.e. seeing what the finalist decks for a certain year looked
like and how they were played) overrides the "personal bad" of one
person not being able to keep their deck private. It's a matter of
opionion, of course, and other tournament organizers will have
different priorities there. That's fine.

What I think *is* important (as I said earlier) is making stuff like
this clear in the tournament announcement. I a certain tournament says
that the winner deck list will become public and you absolutely do not
want your newest invention to become public, then you just need to
skip that tournament. It's a matter of choice, on both parts.

-Petri

Well, we're going round and round on this. I'd assert that there is
also little benefit to hiding your decklist. There are arguments to be
made for both sides here. It comes down to whether you want to require
decklists from finalists (or winner) or just ask for them. It may be a
silly distinction to *you*, but in this your mileage *does* vary ;).

Some people (me included) think requiring deck lists from everyone in
the tournament (before the tournament) is a bit silly. However, when
some tournaments (EC etc) require that, I go along with it (as a
player), no question. Because it's the organizers' call

Again, I think the most important thing here is to make stuff like
that clear to everyone attending. Different places and different
tournament have different styles and expectations, and as long as they
conform to the official tournament rules and rulings, people are free
to run their tournaments in whichever way they choose.

And "scary judge dude"? Not really, generally. I've run these things
for 10-ish years or so, and (imho) have been very laid back about it
and the atmosphere has been very relaxed and sportsmanlike. I don't
see this one communication glitch changing that.

-Petri

Sure.

> Some people (me included) think requiring deck lists from everyone in
> the tournament (before the tournament) is a bit silly. However, when
> some tournaments (EC etc) require that, I go along with it (as a
> player), no question. Because it's the organizers' call

It's the organizer's call and it's another thing which is not a cut-
and-dried issue. But it's not for the same purpose and hence makes a
poor analogy for this issue. I believe requiring decklists at the start
of a tournament is generally a thing done to insure the integrity of the
tournament; to help insure that players aren't altering their decks in
response to the metagame of the tournament once they have information.
Your decklist issue is completely different. As I understand it, it's
just to spiff up your tournament report. It's a "nice" thing, but
hardly worth getting hard-assed about (IMHO, at least).

> Again, I think the most important thing here is to make stuff like
> that clear to everyone attending.

Agreed; this is always a very good thing.

> And "scary judge dude"? Not really, generally. I've run these things
> for 10-ish years or so, and (imho) have been very laid back about it
> and the atmosphere has been very relaxed and sportsmanlike.

I'm just saying, you usually shouldn't need to do anything in
particular to get players to get you their decklists - especially in
a tournament with 10 or more people in it which will therefore land
in the TWDA. In most of those cases, I'd expect the winner to be
chasing you around waving it at you to get it published. (One of the
players in San Fransisco, Ian Lee, actually once mentioned that he
didn't think sanctioning a VEKN tournament with fewer than 10 players
in it was worth bothering with because the winner wouldn't get his
decklist in the TWDA.) So if the occasional player wants to be shy
about it, it doesn't strike me as a big deal.

Fred

Messages.Author: John Whelan
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott wrote:
> It's the organizer's call and it's another thing which is not a cut-
> and-dried issue. But it's not for the same purpose and hence makes a
> poor analogy for this issue. I believe requiring decklists at the start
> of a tournament is generally a thing done to insure the integrity of the
> tournament; to help insure that players aren't altering their decks in
> response to the metagame of the tournament once they have information.
> Your decklist issue is completely different. As I understand it, it's
> just to spiff up your tournament report. It's a "nice" thing, but
> hardly worth getting hard-assed about (IMHO, at least).

As you note, a judge/organizer has the right to demand deck-list
information before the start of play, and this is, in part, a
safeguard against cheating. If you demand the deck-list later, and/or
publish the deck-list after the tournament, this also serves as a
safeguard against cheating -- though perhaps not by itself as
effectively as demanding all information in advance.

Obviously, demanding decks from everyone, in advance, is more of a
hassle for all concerned. But I support the organizer's right to do
this, just as I support his right to take lesser measures, according
to his judgment.

Bottom line is, nobody should be giving the judge a hard time, or
calling him a "bit of a jerk" or a "hard-ass", for demanding and
publishing deck-list information.

> effectively as demanding all information in advance.

A) That's kind of a far-fetched safeguard; but more importantly,...
B) It's not why Petri says he's doing it. We can only judge the
purposes of his rules by what he says the purposes are.Hence my
distinction in the context is valid.

...

> Bottom line is, nobody should be giving the judge a hard time, or
> calling him a "bit of a jerk" or a "hard-ass", for demanding and
> publishing deck-list information.

The "bit of a jerk" thing was Eric's wording not mine. To be sure,
I'm fine with the to-each-his-own attitude about this issue; I'm
just saying I disagree with how far Petri goes with it: it's not
necessary and it even has some negative implications (players may
choose to pass on Petri's tournaments, reducing participation, if
they don't care for his rule), albeit admittedly far-fetched ones.

"Hard-ass" is an accurate description of the situation and not
a flame (nor intended as a flame). It means 'extreme'.

Fred

Messages.Author: John Whelan
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott wrote:
> On 8/2/2010 10:55 AM, John Whelan wrote:
> > As you note, a judge/organizer has the right to demand deck-list
> > information before the start of play, and this is, in part, a
> > safeguard against cheating. If you demand the deck-list later, and/or
> > publish the deck-list after the tournament, this also serves as a
> > safeguard against cheating -- though perhaps not by itself as
> > effectively as demanding all information in advance.
>

> A) That's kind of a far-fetched safeguard; [...]

I disagree. Though, of course, it is all relative.

> [...] but more importantly,...

> B) It's not why Petri says he's doing it.

I don't care. The assumption that judges/organizers have a right to
see and to publish deck information is a deterrent to would-be
cheaters regardless of the precise motives of the judges organizers as
to individual players.

An organizer should not be obliged to make an allegation of cheating
before he has the right to see and publish deck information. This
would only make cheaters feel safer.

> We can only judge the purposes of his rules by what he says the purposes
> are.

I disagree. He is part of a broader V:tES community. The deterrent
function served by rules such as these transcend his precise motives.
If he enforces his prerogative against a recalcitrant player, he sets
an example that makes would-be cheaters feel less safe, regardless of
whether he has the slightest suspicion of cheating by the recalcitrant
player.

> "Hard-ass" is an accurate description of the situation and not
> a flame (nor intended as a flame). It means 'extreme'.

Fine. But I disagree. I don't think Petri has been extreme at all.
